rejection

/rih-JEK-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Rejection means the act of turning down or turning away something or someone — a dismissal of what is offered, proposed, or submitted.

The gallery's rejection of her paintings stung, but the young artist kept submitting new work anyway.

Example

The journal's rejection of Dr. Okafor's first paper came with detailed notes, so he strengthened the experiment and resubmitted six months later.

The journal refused to accept the paper — that refusal itself is the rejection. Notice that rejection is the noun for the act of turning something down, and it often lands on things submitted for judgment: papers, applications, proposals.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dismissal: Dismissal means turning something away as unworthy of consideration — a judge dismisses a case, a critic dismisses an idea with a wave. Rejection at least weighs what was offered before turning it down: a manuscript can be read carefully and still meet rejection. Dismissal implies the weighing never really happened.

denial: Denial means declaring something untrue or declining to grant something asked of you — you deny an accusation, or deny a request that was yours to rule on. Rejection turns down something offered or submitted to you: applications, proposals, manuscripts. A denial says 'that is false' or 'you may not'; a rejection says 'we are not taking this.'

rebuff: A rebuff is a blunt, chilly turning-away of an approach or offer, felt person to person in the moment. Rejection is the broader act of turning down whatever is offered or submitted — from paintings to applications — and it can be delivered kindly. Every rebuff is a rejection served cold.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

acceptance: agreeing to receive or approve

approval: official agreement or favorable judgment

Where it sits · how emphatic the dismissal is

refusal → rejection → repudiation

refusal vs. rejection: A refusal is simply the act of saying no, and it can be quite gentle — milder than a rejection, which dismisses what was offered outright.

repudiation vs. rejection: A repudiation is a forceful, public rejection that disowns something completely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: back (Latin)

Root — ject: to throw (Latin jacere)

Suffix — -ion: act or result of

Put it together: re- + ject + -ion literally means 'the act of throwing back' — when you face rejection, what you offered has been thrown back at you.

Use the root in a new word: trajectory: The outfielder read the ball's trajectory in an instant and made the catch look easy.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Rejection works for things submitted for judgment (applications, manuscripts, proposals) and for people, where it carries a real emotional sting. Medicine borrows it too: a patient's body can show 'organ rejection' when it refuses to accept a transplant — the same core idea of refusing to accept something new.
